name: California Condor
range: Reintroduced to California, Arizona, Utah and Baja California
tagline: North America's largest land bird, saved from the brink
lede: With wings spanning 3 metres, the California condor can glide for kilometres without a single flap. In 1987 it vanished from the wild entirely, when the last free birds were caught to save the species. Today, after one of the most ambitious rescue efforts ever attempted, condors once again ride the thermals over canyons and coastal mountains.
home:
Five hundred years ago, California condors roamed the American Southwest and the West Coast, and in the ice age they ranged across North America, with bones found as far east as southern Florida. When the giant ice age mammals died out, the condor's range shrank with them.

Today, released birds live in the coastal mountains of California, in northern Arizona and southern Utah, including the Grand Canyon area and Zion National Park, and in northern Baja California in Mexico. They favour rocky shrubland, coniferous forest and oak savanna, usually near cliffs or big trees for nesting. Two sanctuaries, the Sisquoc and the Sespe, were set aside for their prime nesting habitat.
anatomy:
This is the largest land bird in North America. Its wingspan is the widest of any bird on the continent, and at up to 14 kg it is almost as heavy as the trumpeter swan. Adults are black with big white triangles under the wings, a frill of black feathers at the base of the neck, an ivory bill and brownish red eyes. The head is largely bald, its skin grey in young birds and yellow to bright orange in breeding adults. Juveniles are mottled dark brown.

Its large flight muscles are not anchored to a matching large breastbone, so the condor is built for soaring rather than flapping. It flaps to take off, then rides rising warm air near cliffs, reaching speeds of 90 km/h and heights of 4,600 metres.
life:
Condors are scavengers. They prefer the carcasses of large mammals such as deer, cattle, horses and sheep, even bears and cougars, but will also eat rabbits, squirrels, salmon, sea lions and stranded whales. With no sense of smell, they find food by watching for eagles and smaller vultures, then use their size to push in. Bears ignore them, and golden eagles will fight them for a meal.

A wild condor may travel 250 km in a day in search of food. It eats irregularly, sometimes going up to two weeks without a meal, then gorging on 1 to 1.5 kg of meat at once. Between flights, condors roost on high perches from which they can launch with little effort.
family:
Condors reach maturity at about 6 years old. In courtship, the male flushes his head red, puffs out his neck feathers, spreads his wings and slowly approaches the female. If she lowers her head, the pair bond for life. They nest in caves or cliff clefts, where the female lays a single bluish-white egg, weighing about 280 grams, every other year.

Both parents incubate it for 53 to 60 days. Chicks hatch with their eyes open, wear grey down until they are nearly adult-sized, and fly at 5 to 6 months, but stay with their parents into their second year. If an egg is lost, the parents lay another, a habit breeders use to double the number of chicks. Condors can live up to 60 years, making them some of the longest-lived birds in the world.
remarkable: In 2021, scientists at the San Diego Zoo revealed that two condor chicks hatched in its breeding programme, in 2001 and 2009, had no father. Genetic tests showed they had developed from unfertilised eggs, by a process called parthenogenesis, even though their mothers lived with males and had mated before. In the earlier known cases in birds, the embryos had all died before hatching.
outlook:
The California condor is listed as Critically Endangered by the IUCN. In the 20th century, poaching, the pesticide DDT, lead poisoning and habitat loss drove numbers so low that the US government captured every remaining wild bird by 1987, leaving a population of just 27. Bred at the San Diego Wild Animal Park and the Los Angeles Zoo, condors were released again from 1991, and by December 2016 there were 446 birds, 276 of them wild. In 2015, for the first time, more condors were born in the wild than died.

Lead from bullet fragments in carcasses remains the main killer of juveniles and adults, and California has required hunters in condor range to use non-lead ammunition since 2008. Nestlings often die after their parents feed them bits of rubbish mistaken for bone, and captive-bred birds are now trained to avoid power lines and people.
people:
The condor features in the stories of many Native American peoples, in strikingly different roles. For the Wiyot of California, the condor recreated humankind after a great flood, while the Mono told of a destroyer that drained human blood. The Yokuts said the condor sometimes ate the moon, and the Chumash said it was once a white bird that turned black after flying too close to a fire.

Condor feather headdresses and bones have been found in Native American graves, and some tribes ritually killed condors for ceremonial clothing. During the California Gold Rush, some condors were even kept as pets. The modern rescue has been one of the most expensive conservation projects in US history, costing over $35 million.
relatives:
The California condor is a New World vulture and the only living member of its genus, Gymnogyps, from the Greek for 'naked vulture'. George Shaw described it in 1797, placing it in the same genus as the Andean condor of South America, but it was later given a genus of its own. The word condor comes from kuntur in Quechua.

Fossils show that Gymnogyps was once widespread across the Americas, with extinct relatives described from Florida, Peru and Cuba. A larger ice age form, sometimes treated as a separate species, was about as heavy as the Andean condor and had a wider bill.
didYouKnow: In 2024 the Los Angeles Zoo reported a record 17 condor chicks in one breeding season, using a method in which one adult raises 2 or 3 chicks at once.

quiz.prompt: How did the California condor disappear from the wild in 1987?
choices: A wildfire destroyed the final nesting cliffs in the Sespe sanctuary
quiz.explanation: The US government caught every remaining wild condor to breed them in captivity.

quiz.prompt: How does a condor find carcasses, given it has no sense of smell?
choices: By following scent trails left on the wind by rotting meat
quiz.explanation: It looks for eagles and smaller vultures gathering at a carcass, then muscles in.

quiz.prompt: How often does a mated female condor lay an egg?
choices: Three or four times a year, in different cliff caves
quiz.explanation: A female lays one egg every other year, which makes recovery slow.

charities.blurb: Protects birds and the places they need across the Americas.

name: Devils Hole Pupfish
range: A single water-filled cavern in Nevada's Amargosa Valley
tagline: A fish whose entire world is one desert pool
lede: Every wild Devils Hole pupfish lives in one flooded crack in the Nevada desert, a pool roughly the size of a large room at the surface. It may be the smallest habitat on Earth to hold the whole population of a vertebrate species. Few fish have been fought over so fiercely, all the way to the US Supreme Court.
home:
Devils Hole is a water-filled cavern running into a hillside in the Amargosa Valley of southwestern Nevada, east of Death Valley, at 730 metres above sea level. Its surface measures roughly 22 by 3.5 metres, but it plunges at least 130 metres deep. The water stays at 33 °C all year and holds little oxygen.

The pupfish live only in the top 24 metres and are most numerous above 15 metres. Their lifeline is a small rock shelf, about 3.5 by 5 metres, lying around 30 centimetres below the surface at one end. Sunlight on the shelf grows the algae that feed the whole system, and almost all feeding and spawning happens there. Barn owls roosting in the cave may add nutrients, as their pellets drop into the water.
anatomy:
At up to 30 mm long, with an average of 23 mm, this is the smallest pupfish in its genus. Males are dark brown with metallic blue sides, black-edged fins, a golden sheen on the back and gill covers with a violet tint. Females and young are more yellow, with metallic green gill covers and blue-tinted eyes, and the young have a faint vertical bar on each side.

Unlike its relatives, the Devils Hole pupfish has no pelvic fins. Curiously, fish raised in cooler water in captivity have been seen to grow them.
life:
In such a tiny world, the pupfish eats almost anything available: diatoms and other algae, tiny crustaceans, protozoa, beetles, flatworms and snails. Its diet shifts with the seasons, and its stomach nearly always contains particles of travertine, a form of limestone, swallowed as it picks food from the bottom and the surface.

Its enemies include a predatory diving beetle that eats its eggs and young, first recorded in Devils Hole in 1999 or 2000. Numbers rise and fall each year with the algae on the shelf, so spring counts are often only a third to two thirds of the autumn ones.
family:
Pupfish spawn all year round, with a peak from mid-February to mid-May and a smaller one from July to September. Females are not very fertile: an average female may produce only 4 or 5 mature eggs a season, probably releasing just one at each spawning. The eggs are only 1 mm across, few hatch, and few young survive.

An adult lives just 10 to 14 months, so the population depends on each year's breeding going well.
remarkable: Earthquakes far away can shake Devils Hole. Big quakes in Mexico in 2012, Alaska in 2018 and California in 2019 set the water sloshing in standing waves called seiches, which scour algae, eggs and larvae from the shelf. The fish respond by fleeing en masse into the depths and then spawning out of season. Several males chase a lone female until she lets one swim beside her, and he fertilises her egg the moment she lays it.
outlook:
The Devils Hole pupfish has been listed as endangered in the US since 1967, among the first species protected under the Endangered Species Act, and as Critically Endangered by the IUCN since 2014. In the late 1960s, wells pumping groundwater for nearby farms lowered the pool and exposed the vital shelf. The population recovered, then went into a second, unexplained decline from 1995, and it swings wildly: 35 fish in April 2013, 263 in September 2022, and just 20 in spring 2025 after two earthquakes, before 19 captive-bred fish were added for the first time.

In the early 2010s, a full-size replica of the top 6.7 metres of Devils Hole, holding 380,000 litres, was built less than 2 km away. Raised from eggs collected in winter, its backup population is considered very successful, unlike earlier refuges, which all failed.
people:
Ichthyologist Carl Hubbs campaigned in the late 1940s to protect the fish, and in 1952 President Harry Truman made Devils Hole part of Death Valley National Monument. When a ranching company drilled wells nearby, the dispute reached the Supreme Court, which ruled in 1976 in Cappaert v. United States that protecting the monument had also reserved enough groundwater for the pupfish.

The fight split local opinion. One magazine said that letting the fish die would be like bombing the Louvre to make way for a parking lot, while rival bumper stickers read 'Save the Pupfish' and 'Kill the Pupfish'. In 2016, three men broke in and waded onto the shelf, smashing eggs and larvae, and a pupfish died; the site now has extra fencing, sensors and cameras.
relatives:
The species was described in 1930 by Joseph Wales, and its name, diabolis, refers to Devils Hole, which is officially spelled without an apostrophe. It belongs to the pupfish family, Cyprinodontidae. Its closest relative is Cyprinodon nevadensis, and together with the Death Valley pupfish the three form a group from the Amargosa River basin.

How long it has lived in Devils Hole is hotly debated. The cavern formed about 60,000 years ago, and estimates of the fish's age range from that down to less than 1,000 years. Nobody knows how it got there; one idea is that Native Americans, who ate pupfish, carried it in.
didYouKnow: A flash flood in 2004 swept scientific monitoring equipment into Devils Hole, killing an estimated 80 pupfish.

quiz.prompt: Which fins does the Devils Hole pupfish lack?
choices: Pectoral fins, so it must rest on the shallow shelf
quiz.explanation: A defining trait of the species is its lack of pelvic fins.

quiz.prompt: What did the Supreme Court decide in Cappaert v. United States?
choices: Water was reserved for the fish
The pool should be drained and the fish moved to a hatchery in Arizona
quiz.explanation: It ruled that protecting the monument implicitly reserved enough groundwater for the pupfish.

quiz.prompt: How long does a Devils Hole pupfish usually live?
choices: Up to 60 years, thanks to the warm, stable water
quiz.explanation: Individuals live just 10 to 14 months.

name: Burying Beetle
range: Northern Europe and Asia to Japan, plus Alaska and northwestern Canada
tagline: A beetle that buries the dead to raise its young
lede: When a small mammal or bird dies in a northern wood, a pair of these orange-and-black beetles may soon have it underground, stripped and embalmed. The carcass becomes a nursery and larder for their young, and, unusually for insects, mother and father both stay to feed them.
home:
This burying beetle is found across the northern Palearctic, from the far north of Scandinavia through Siberia to China and Japan, and in North America in Alaska and northwestern Canada. In Europe and Asia it lives everywhere from lowland plains to alpine heights, in dense woodland, open heath, parks and even gardens; in North America it keeps to open forest.

Adults wake from dormancy around April and May. Their activity peaks in May, with a second surge in late summer, and carries on into late autumn.
anatomy:
Adults vary a lot in size, from 12 to 20 mm long. Each wing case carries two bright orange-yellow bands on black, and the wing cases are squarish and shorter than the abdomen, leaving its tip exposed. The antennae are completely black, an important feature for telling it apart from similar species.

The bold colours warn birds that the beetle is not worth attacking, a strategy called aposematism, and males and females differ somewhat in their colouring and chemical defences. When threatened, the beetle oozes a fluid from its abdomen that also helps it fight microbes. It flies well, which it needs to do to find carcasses.
life:
Adults depend on dead vertebrates. Finding a suitable small carcass triggers a surge of juvenile hormone that switches the beetles into breeding mode. Their genome holds very few genes for breaking down plant material, and instead they rely on a close partnership with their gut microbes, which help them digest carrion, cope with its toxins and hold back spoilage and competing microbes.

Their immune system is tuned to this risky way of life. An enzyme called phenoloxidase, important both for immunity and for hardening the beetle's outer skin, becomes more active during breeding, and can be boosted further if the beetle is injured.
family:
A pair works together to bury the carcass, strip off its fur or feathers and shape it into a compact ball, which they coat with antimicrobial secretions to slow its decay. The female lays eggs in the soil nearby, and a few days later the larvae hatch and crawl to the carcass, their nursery and food supply.

Both parents then feed the larvae pre-digested food and guard them against predators and rivals. If one parent leaves or slacks off, the other works harder to make up for it, and it is very rare for both to desert. Their choices seem to be negotiated through repeated interactions rather than made by one partner alone. Young raised on fresher, less decayed carcasses grow better and are healthier.
remarkable: Tiny mites hitch rides on these beetles from carcass to carcass. The largest, Poecilochirus carabi, simply roams over the beetle's body rather than clinging on, and was long thought to be a helpful passenger that ate the eggs and larvae of rival flies. Researchers have since shown that adult mites also eat the beetle's own eggs, harming its breeding, so the partnership is not as friendly as it once seemed.
outlook:
Its huge range across the northern hemisphere, and its ability to live in habitats from wild heathland to suburban gardens, point to a hardy and adaptable insect. Its conservation status has not been formally evaluated.

Its breeding does rely on a steady supply of small dead animals, and on soil it can dig into to bury them.
people:
Nicrophorus vespilloides is one of the most studied burying beetles, with over 1,000 citations in the scientific literature. It is a model organism for research on social immunity, the ways animals protect their family or group from disease. Scientists also use it to explore parental care, conflict between mates and between siblings, and the genes behind these behaviours.

The species was described by Johann Friedrich Wilhelm Herbst in 1783.
relatives:
Burying beetles of the genus Nicrophorus share the habit of burying carcasses for their young. A close relative, Nicrophorus nepalensis, breeds in much the same way, though the details vary with habitat.

In 2016, researchers found that beetles long counted as this species in central and eastern Canada and the northeastern United States were actually a separate, overlooked sister species, Nicrophorus hebes, first named back in 1837. It is restricted to sphagnum bogs and marshes, possibly pushed there by competition with another relative, N. defodiens, which lives in the surrounding forests.
didYouKnow: Near Ottawa, researchers have never found the bog specialist in woodland even 100 metres beyond the edge of the Mer Bleue bog.

quiz.prompt: What does a pair of these beetles do with a small carcass?
choices: Bury it as food for their young
Leave it for flies and feed their young on the maggots
quiz.explanation: They bury it, strip it, roll it into a ball and coat it with antimicrobials for their larvae.

quiz.prompt: What colour are this beetle's antennae?
choices: Bright green with yellow bands to match its wing cases
quiz.explanation: Its totally black antennae are an important distinguishing feature.

quiz.prompt: What happens if one parent stops caring for the larvae?
choices: The remaining parent eats the brood and flies off to a fresh carcass
quiz.explanation: The remaining partner compensates by stepping up its own care.

name: Common Vampire Bat
range: Mexico through Central and South America to Uruguay and Chile
tagline: A blood-drinking bat that shares its meals with friends
lede: The common vampire bat really does drink blood, creeping up on sleeping animals in the dark and lapping from a tiny wound. Yet this small, much-feared creature is one of the most social of all bats, grooming its roost-mates and even feeding those that come home hungry.
home:
It lives in parts of Mexico, Central America and South America, reaching as far north as 280 km south of the US border and as far south as Uruguay, northern Argentina and central Chile. Offshore, it is found on the islands of Trinidad and Margarita. Fossils show it once lived in Florida and in the states bordering Mexico. In southeastern Brazil it is the most common bat of all.

It prefers warm, humid climates and forages over tropical and subtropical woodland and open grassland. By day it roosts in trees, caves, abandoned buildings, old wells and mines, alongside some 45 other bat species, usually claiming the darkest, highest spots. When the vampires leave, other bats move into their places.
anatomy:
This is a small bat, about 9 cm long with a wingspan of 18 cm, usually weighing 25 to 40 grams, though a single meal can make it much heavier. Its fur is short, darker on the back and silver-grey below, and it has a flat, leaf-shaped nose and a deeply grooved lower lip. A strong, clawed thumb on each wing helps it climb onto prey and take off.

It has the fewest teeth of any bat, just 18, and its short snout makes room for large incisors and canines. The upper incisors lack enamel, which keeps them razor-sharp. It has good eyesight and keen senses of smell and hearing, and it echolocates through its mouth, so it flies with its mouth open.
life:
Vampire bats hunt at night, using echolocation and smell to find prey within 5 to 8 km of the roost. Their main hosts are livestock, especially cattle and horses, and given the choice they prefer horses, though they also feed on wild animals such as tapirs. A bat lands on its target, or hops up from the ground, usually at the rump, flank or neck. Heat sensors in its nose find blood vessels near the skin, its teeth bite away a small flap, and it laps the flowing blood with a grooved tongue.

Its saliva contains an anticoagulant called draculin, named after Count Dracula, which stops the blood clotting. Feeding bats guard their host and chase off other bats, and only mothers and their young tend to share one animal.
family:
Dominant males guard roosts that attract groups of females, though females often switch between roosts. Vampires breed all year, with a peak in the rainy season. After a pregnancy of about 7 months, a female gives birth to a single pup, which she raises largely on her own. She leaves it behind to hunt and calls to it to feed when she returns.

Young bats join their mothers on hunts at 6 months but are not fully weaned until 9 months. Daughters usually stay in the group they were born into, while sons leave at 1 to 2 years old, sometimes driven out by the resident adult males.
remarkable: A vampire bat that fails to feed can be rescued by a roost-mate, which regurgitates some of its own blood meal. In a field study in Costa Rica, 95% of the sharing seen in the wild was between close kin, and 70% was mothers feeding pups. Yet sharing between adults is predicted even better by how much time two bats spend together, and bats give most to those that have given to them, a reciprocity built over long friendships. Bats that share food also groom each other, and grooming may let a bat check whether its partner's belly really is empty.
outlook:
The common vampire bat is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, thanks to its wide distribution, its presumed large population and its tolerance of some habitat change. It is not thought to be declining anywhere near fast enough to be threatened.

Far from needing protection, it is often treated as a pest, because it feeds on livestock and can carry rabies.
people:
In March 1932, Joseph Lennox Pawan, a government bacteriologist in Trinidad, found the first vampire bat infected with rabies. He went on to show that bats can carry and pass on the disease for long periods without showing symptoms, a finding at first ridiculed as fantastic. Rabies is most common in the large vampire populations of South America, where the danger is mainly to livestock rather than people, though anyone who wakes to find a vampire bat in their bedroom should seek medical care.

The bat's saliva has also given something back. A genetically engineered drug called desmoteplase, based on its anticoagulant, has been shown to increase blood flow in stroke patients.
relatives:
This is one of three living vampire bats, all in the subfamily Desmodontinae, along with the hairy-legged and white-winged vampire bats. All three feed on the blood of warm-blooded animals, but the other two mainly target birds, while the common vampire prefers mammals. It can be told apart by its longer thumb. These 'true' vampires are distinct from the so-called false vampire bats.

The species was first described in 1810 by Étienne Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire and received its current name, Desmodus rotundus, from Oldfield Thomas in 1901. It is the only living member of its genus, though fossil species are known.
didYouKnow: Unlike most bats, vampire bats can run, bounding along the ground by pushing off with their powerful wings rather than their legs.

quiz.prompt: Who is the anticoagulant in vampire bat saliva named after?
choices: The Greek word for blood, because it keeps blood flowing
quiz.explanation: It is called draculin, after Count Dracula.

quiz.prompt: Which livestock do common vampire bats prefer when given the choice?
choices: Pigs kept in open pens near the forest edge
quiz.explanation: They feed on cattle and horses but favour horses.

quiz.prompt: How many teeth does the common vampire bat have?
quiz.explanation: It has just 18 teeth, the fewest of any bat.

name: Pyrosome
range: Warm open oceans worldwide, mostly between 50°N and 50°S
tagline: A glowing tube of tiny animals drifting the open ocean
lede: A pyrosome looks like one glowing pickle drifting through the dark sea, but it is really a colony of many tiny animals living together in a shared jelly tube. Disturb one and waves of blue-green light ripple along its body. Most are under 60 centimetres long, but giants grow big enough for divers to swim inside.
home:
Pyrosomes have been recorded in every ocean except the Arctic, usually between 50°N and 50°S. Most live in the upper layers of warm seas, though some are found deeper. They are planktonic, carried mostly by currents, tides and waves.

Many move up and down the water column each day, and they have been found from 20 metres to more than 700 metres deep. The daily journey varies widely, from 20 metres to more than 500 metres, and most sightings happen near the surface at night. Some species appear to be expanding their range as the oceans warm, and their distribution may also shift with the seasons.
anatomy:
Each colony is made of individual animals called zooids, typically only a few millimetres long, bound together by a tunic of shared tissue into a hollow tube. Colonies are usually between about 2.5 and 60 centimetres long, with walls 0.2 to 2 centimetres thick, but giants can reach about 18 metres, with an opening 2 metres wide. One species, Pyrostremma spinosum, can grow to 20 metres.

The colony is transparent and gelatinous, slimy but bumpy, with each zooid showing as a small bump. Their stomachs, visible through the clear body, have been compared to wire baskets. Most colonies are finger-shaped, though two species are more rounded, and the outer covering ranges from limp to tough and elastic.
life:
Each zooid opens both outside and inside the tube. It draws seawater in through a filtering mesh called the branchial basket, strains out microscopic plant cells and other particles, and pushes the filtered water into the hollow centre. Pyrosomes are among the most efficient filter feeders in the zooplankton, and a colony may be 50 million times heavier than the particles it eats.

The beating of tiny hairs called cilia in all the baskets together creates the feeding current and also drives the colony slowly forward by jet propulsion. Pyrosomes in turn are eaten by at least 62 open-ocean animals, including turtles and sea lions, and at least 33 seabed animals, such as sea urchins and crabs, as well as by seabirds, fish and whales.
family:
Pyrosomes are hermaphrodites with a two-stage life cycle. A fertilised egg develops into a first individual, called a cyathozooid, which then buds off a group of 4 zooids. As a colony grows, more zooids are added: in swirls in one genus, in neat parallel rows in another, and in a dense, random jumble in the third.

A colony can fertilise itself from one end of the tube to the other. Zooids near the closed end produce male cells before female ones, while those near the open end do the reverse.
remarkable: Pyrosome light comes from bacteria living inside the animals' own cells. Each zooid has a pair of light organs packed with these bacteria, which are thought to be controlled by their host, something rarely seen in other glowing sea creatures. Each zooid can sense light and flash in response, so waves of light pass back and forth along the colony, visible from many tens of metres away. The glow may be used to signal danger or to communicate with neighbouring colonies.
outlook:
Far from dwindling, pyrosomes can multiply explosively in events called blooms. In 2017, they spread in unprecedented numbers along the Pacific coast of North America as far north as Alaska, possibly helped by several years of unusually warm coastal water. Warming seas may make such blooms more common.

Blooms can upset food webs, as vast numbers of pyrosomes graze down the phytoplankton other animals need, and scientists feared that a mass die-off could create a dead zone as rotting colonies used up the oxygen in the water. Yet pyrosomes are also rich in energy, and dead colonies sinking to the seabed feed deep-sea animals and carry carbon down with them.
people:
Pyrosomes have plenty of nicknames: sea pickles, for their tube-like shape, as well as sea worms, sea squirts, fire bodies, fire salps and cockroaches of the sea. The scientific name Pyrosoma comes from the Greek words for 'fire' and 'body'.

Sailors occasionally report calm night seas filled with pyrosomes, all glowing at once.
relatives:
Pyrosomes are free-floating tunicates, a group of filter-feeding sea animals, and are close relatives of salps. The family Pyrosomatidae contains eight species in three genera, Pyrosoma, Pyrosomella and Pyrostremma, split between two subfamilies.

The genera can be told apart by the projections on their outer covering: spiny and triangular in Pyrostremma, smooth in Pyrosomella, and long and blunt in Pyrosoma. Pyrosoma and Pyrosomella also have a ring of muscle called a colonial sphincter, or diaphragm, which Pyrostremma lacks.
didYouKnow: About 35% of a pyrosome's dry weight is carbon, which is high for a jelly-bodied animal.

quiz.prompt: What makes a pyrosome glow?
choices: Tiny crystals it absorbs from the algae it filters out of the sea
quiz.explanation: Each zooid's light organs are packed with bioluminescent bacteria living inside its cells.

quiz.prompt: What is a pyrosome?
choices: A floating seaweed that is home to many tiny glowing shrimps
quiz.explanation: It is a colony of zooids bound together in a shared gelatinous tube.

quiz.prompt: Which animals are pyrosomes closely related to?
choices: Octopuses and squid, which also glow
quiz.explanation: Pyrosomes are tunicates and close relatives of salps, sometimes called fire salps.

name: Green Anaconda
range: Tropical South America east of the Andes, from Trinidad to Paraguay
tagline: The world's heaviest snake, waiting in the shallows
lede: The green anaconda is the heaviest snake on Earth, a giant constrictor that lurks almost unseen in the rivers and swamps of South America. Females dwarf the males, and a big one can outweigh a grown person. Its real size is impressive enough, yet the legends have grown even faster.
home:
Green anacondas live in South America east of the Andes, in countries including Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Brazil and the Guianas, from the island of Trinidad south to northern Paraguay. They favour tropical rainforest and especially shallow, slow-moving water: streams, rivers and flooded grasslands such as the llanos. They spend most of their time in the water, but also move through thick vegetation on land.

As of August 2023, 11 green anacondas had been verifiably seen in the wild in Florida, spread over more than 560 km. No breeding population is known there, but the state added the species to its list of prohibited non-native animals in 2021 and rates its risks as very high.
anatomy:
Mature females typically reach up to 5 metres, averaging about 4.6 metres, while males average about 3 metres, and adults usually weigh 30 to 80 kg. The longest reliably recorded reach about 6.3 metres. Herpetologist Jesús Rivas, who examined more than 900 anacondas, found the biggest to be a 5.21-metre female weighing 97.5 kg. It is slightly shorter than the reticulated python but far bulkier: a 5.2-metre anaconda is as hefty as a 7.4-metre python.

Its skin is olive green with black blotches, and orange-yellow stripes usually run along each side of its narrow head. Its jaw bones are joined at the front by stretchy ligaments, so it can swallow prey wider than its own head, and an opening of the windpipe in its mouth lets it breathe while swallowing.
life:
Mostly active at night, the anaconda is a fast swimmer that floats underwater with only its eyes and nostrils, set high on its head, above the surface. When prey passes close, it strikes, wraps around it, suffocates it and swallows it whole. Digestion takes many days, during which the snake is sluggish.

An apex predator, it takes almost anything it can overpower: fish, amphibians, birds, mammals and reptiles. Prey is often 14 to 50% of its own weight, from capybaras and caimans to turtles, peccaries and deer, and the largest anacondas occasionally manage tapirs and even jaguars. Big prey can injure or kill it, a risk it may reduce by drowning its victim. Even adults are eaten by Orinoco crocodiles, black caimans and jaguars.
family:
Anacondas are solitary until the mating season in the rainy months, usually around April and May. Females leave pheromone trails, and many males may converge on one female from all directions. Up to 12 males can wrap around her in a breeding ball, wrestling in slow motion for 2 to 4 weeks and scratching her with small spurs.

After a gestation of 6 to 7 months, the female gives birth to live young, usually 20 to 40 but sometimes as many as 100, and may lose up to half her weight. The newborns, 70 to 80 cm long, get no parental care. Anacondas live about 10 years in the wild and 30 or more in captivity, where one reached 37 years and 317 days.
remarkable: Female anacondas sometimes eat males. Most recorded cases of cannibalism involve a large female eating a smaller male, perhaps because she needs food to sustain her long pregnancy and he is simply nearby. Females can also reproduce without males at all: in 2014, a green anaconda at West Midland Safari Park gave birth to 3 young by parthenogenesis.
outlook:
Green anacondas still occupy a vast area of South America, and the biggest live deep in remote parts of the Amazon. That remoteness also makes them hard to study. Transporting huge specimens is difficult, skins can stretch by more than 50% when tanned, and even trained scientists tend to overestimate a snake before it is measured.

Where they have escaped or been released, as in Florida, anacondas are a worry for native wildlife. Authorities there fear they could compete with native predators and eat animals such as white-tailed deer, American alligators, crocodiles and wading birds.
people:
The Guinness Book of World Records says this species may have been subject to the most extreme size exaggerations of any living animal. The naturalists Henry Walter Bates and Alfred Russel Wallace heard rumours of anacondas 9 to 12 metres long, but only saw snakes of about 6 metres. In Guyana in 1937, zoologist Alpheus Hyatt Verrill asked his team to guess the length of a coiled anaconda: guesses ran from 6.1 to 18.3 metres, and it measured 5.9 metres.

Horror films often show it as a man-eater, but there is no verified case of a green anaconda eating a person, possibly because the largest live far from people. The local Carib peoples called it akayima, 'the great snake', long before scientists described it, and other names include water boa and sucuri.
relatives:
The green anaconda belongs to the boa family, Boidae, and like all boas it is a non-venomous constrictor. It is the largest snake native to the Americas. Linnaeus first named it Boa murina in 1758, based on a description of a spotted American snake that lies in wait for mice, and in 1830 Johann Georg Wagler gave it its own genus, Eunectes. The species name murinus means 'of mice'.

Several proposals to split off new species or subspecies, most recently Eunectes akayima in 2024, are now treated as part of the green anaconda.
didYouKnow: The green anaconda's largest internal organ is its liver.

quiz.prompt: How do green anacondas produce their young?
choices: They give birth to live young
They lay eggs in a nest
They lay eggs inside termite mounds, which keep them warm
quiz.explanation: The species is ovoviviparous, and females give birth to live young.

quiz.prompt: Which sex is larger in green anacondas?
choices: Males, which grow up to twice the length of females
quiz.explanation: Females are generally much larger, averaging about 4.6 metres against about 3 metres for males.

quiz.prompt: What did the guesses in Verrill's 1937 test show?
choices: Coiled snakes always measure longer than they look
quiz.explanation: Guesses ranged up to 18.3 metres for a snake that measured 5.9 metres.

name: Electric Eel
range: Rivers and swamps of northern South America
tagline: A fish that stuns its prey with up to 860 volts
lede: Electric eels can deliver shocks of up to 860 volts, the strongest electricity made by any living thing. They hunt in murky water with poor eyesight, sensing the world through electric fields, and they must rise to the surface to gulp air. And despite the name, they are not eels at all.
home:
The 3 species of electric eel live in northern South America, with largely separate ranges. E. electricus lives in the north, on the Guiana Shield, and E. voltai in the south, from the Brazilian Shield northwards, both in upland waters. E. varii lives in between, mostly in lowlands where streams, grasslands, ravines and ponds swell and shrink with the wet and dry seasons.

All three live on muddy river bottoms and sometimes in swamps, favouring areas in deep shade.
anatomy:
Electric eels have long, stout bodies, rounded at the front and flatter towards the tail. E. electricus can reach 2 metres and 20 kg. The skin is smooth, thick and scaleless, brown to black with a yellow or red belly. Males are larger than females. They swim by rippling a long fin that runs along the underside of the body, supported by more than 400 bony rays.

They have small eyes and poor vision but can hear well. All the vital organs are packed into the front 20% of the body, kept apart from the electric organs. They get most of their oxygen by gulping air about every 2 minutes and absorbing it through a frilled, blood-rich lining in the mouth, and they shed most of their carbon dioxide through the skin. With wet skin, they can survive on land for some hours.
life:
Electric eels are mostly nocturnal and mainly eat fish. E. voltai favours armoured catfish, and one was found with a caecilian, a legless amphibian with toxic skin, in its stomach. E. voltai sometimes hunts in packs, herding a shoal of tetras into a tight mass and then striking together. E. varii also hunts fish, especially armoured catfish and cichlids.

To find prey, an eel uses electroreceptors in patches across its body and a lateral line that senses water movements. A weak discharge of nearly 10 volts is thought to serve for electrolocation. To stun prey, it fires high-voltage pulses as fast as 500 a second, each lasting about 2 milliseconds, and it can curl around its victim to concentrate the shock. In self-defence, eels have been seen leaping from the water to shock animals as big as horses.
family:
Electric eels breed in the dry season, from September to December, when pairs gather in small pools left as the water drops. The male builds a nest from his saliva, and the female lays around 1,200 eggs, adding more batches through the season. The eggs hatch after 7 days, and once the larvae reach 15 mm they eat any leftover eggs, switching to other food at 9 cm.

Males start breeding at 1.2 metres long, females at about 70 cm. Parental care lasts 4 months, with the male guarding the nest and young, though the two upland species seem to rely on it less. Young eels can make electric discharges at just 7 cm long. They keep growing throughout life, adding vertebrae, up to about 300 in all, and captive eels have lived for more than 20 years.
remarkable: An electric eel works like a living battery. It has 3 pairs of electric organs made of cells called electrocytes, which evolved from muscle cells. In the main organ, some 6,000 electrocytes are stacked in series, and around 35 such stacks run in parallel on each side of the body. Each cell adds a little voltage, so together they produce at least 600 volts, with currents of about 1 ampere. Fresh water resists electricity, so a freshwater fish needs a very high voltage to deliver a strong shock, whereas marine electric rays manage with much less.
outlook:
Electric eels are found across a large part of northern South America, and their ability to breathe air lets them survive in shrinking dry-season pools and swamps where many fish could not.

Until 2019, all electric eels were thought to be a single species, so scientists are only beginning to learn how the three species differ in their ranges, habits and needs. Even the names are not quite settled: E. varii may turn out to be the same as a species described from the Peruvian Amazon in 1941.
people:
The Tupi name puraké means 'the one that numbs', and the first written mention, by the Jesuit priest Fernão Cardim, dates from 1583. In 1775, the surgeon John Hunter described the eel's electric organs to the Royal Society, and Hugh Williamson ran experiments showing it shocked fish with the same electricity he felt in his own hand. Their work influenced Luigi Galvani and Alessandro Volta, whose electric battery followed in 1800.

That year Alexander von Humboldt watched indigenous fishers drive about 30 horses into a pool, provoking the eels to leap up and shock them until the fish were exhausted and easy to catch; 2 horses were stunned and drowned. Michael Faraday later measured an eel's shocks with copper paddles, and engineers are now designing artificial electrocytes that might one day power medical implants.
relatives:
Electric eels are knifefish, members of the order Gymnotiformes, and form the subfamily Electrophorinae within the family Gymnotidae. Most knifefish are only weakly electric, using their fields to sense their surroundings but not to shock. The eel's lineage split from its closest relatives, the Gymnotus knifefish, in the Cretaceous.

The genus name Electrophorus means 'electricity bearer'. For more than 200 years it was thought to hold a single species, until a 2019 study split it into three: E. electricus, E. voltai and E. varii.
didYouKnow: In the 1870s the German zoologist Carl Sachs caught electric eels wearing rubber gloves, to the surprise of local people.

quiz.prompt: Which group of fish do electric eels actually belong to?
choices: Lungfish, which also breathe air at the surface
quiz.explanation: They are knifefish of the order Gymnotiformes, not true eels.

quiz.prompt: How does an electric eel get most of its oxygen?
choices: From bubbles trapped in the saliva nest the male builds
quiz.explanation: It breathes air through its mouth about every 2 minutes.

quiz.prompt: In which year were electric eels split into three species?
quiz.explanation: A 2019 study divided them into E. electricus, E. voltai and E. varii.

name: Asian Weaver Ant
range: Tropical Asia from India to the Philippines, and northern Australia
tagline: Ants that sew leaf tents with silk from their own young
lede: Asian weaver ants build their homes high in the trees by pulling living leaves together and stitching them with silk. The thread comes from their own larvae, which workers wave back and forth across the seams like tiny shuttles. A single colony can number half a million ants.
home:
This ant lives in tropical Asia and Australia, from India through Indonesia and the Philippines to the Northern Territory and Queensland. It is arboreal, nesting among the foliage of trees, and is an important part of the canopy ecosystem in humid tropical regions.

A colony may have several nests in one tree or spread across neighbouring trees; one colony occupied 151 nests in 12 trees. Nests are built at night, with major workers weaving the outside and smaller workers finishing the inside. In Singapore, colonies often live in sea hibiscus and great morinda trees, which offer the ants nectar and in return get protection from leaf-eating insects.
anatomy:
Weaver ants come in distinct sizes. Ordinary workers, 5 to 7 mm long, care for the larvae and farm scale insects for honeydew. Major workers, 8 to 10 mm long, have long, strong legs and large jaws, and do the foraging, assembling and expanding of nests. Both are mostly orange. Queens are much bigger, at 20 to 25 mm, and usually greenish-brown, which gives the species its name smaragdina, Latin for emerald.

They do not sting, but their bite is painful, and they can add irritant chemicals from their abdomens into the wound.
life:
Weaver ants hunt insects and other invertebrates, mainly beetles, flies, and wasps and their relatives. They also tend aphids, scale insects and other sap-suckers for their sweet honeydew, driving other ants away from the parts of the canopy where these insects live, especially where trees are linked by lianas. Shelters may even be built close to the nest to protect these assets.

The colony uses a two-level alarm system. Pheromones from one gland gather a local cluster of workers against intruders such as other ants or large insects. If the threat persists, this switches to long-range recruitment, using odour trails from another gland together with touching and body waggling, the same signals that mobilise the colony to claim new territory or exploit food.
family:
Each colony has a single queen, living in one of its nests, and her young are carried to the other nests. A mature colony lives for about 8 years on average.

The colony's brood is a prize for some clever thieves. A jumping spider, Cosmophasis bitaeniata, mimics the ants' chemical scent so it can walk into their nests and eat the larvae. It even lays its own eggs beside the nest, so that its spiderlings can easily reach the ant larvae too.
remarkable: Building a leaf nest takes extraordinary teamwork. Workers spread out and tug at leaf edges independently, and when one manages to bend a leaf, others nearby stop and join it to pull in unison. Where a gap is too wide, they form living chains, climbing onto each other's backs and pulling backwards for leverage. These chains act as a force ratchet: some ants pull while others hold the stored tension using the grip of their feet, which doubles the average force of each ant. In most groups, each member's effort drops as the team grows; here it rises. Once the leaves are in place, some workers hold them while others fetch larvae to spin the silk.
outlook:
Weaver ants are widespread and adaptable, nesting in plantation trees as readily as in forest. In Indonesia, colonies live in banana, coconut, oil palm, rubber, cacao, teak, mango, jackfruit and rambutan trees, among many others. Their conservation status has not been formally evaluated.

Rather than being threatened by people, they are often encouraged by them, and their young are harvested commercially in parts of Asia. Their communication has been called perhaps the most elaborate yet recognised in ants, and one of the most complex systems known among social insects.
people:
People have put weaver ants to work for a very long time. The oldest written record of their use against pests comes from China in 304 CE, where they guarded citrus trees, and colonies still protect crops such as cashew, mango, citrus, coconut, cocoa and coffee. In Sri Lanka, though, ant protection was abandoned in coffee because picking the crop proved too painful.

In Java, the larvae and pupae, called kroto, are sold as food for the island's popular captive songbirds, and mixed with eggs, maize, beans and honey as fishing bait. In Thailand and the Philippines they are eaten, with a taste described as creamy, sour and lemony, and in parts of India the adult ants are used in traditional medicine.
relatives:
The name Oecophylla comes from Greek and means 'leaf-house'. The species has many common names, including weaver ant, green ant, green tree ant and orange gaster.

Several animals have evolved to exploit it. The jumping spider Myrmaplata plataleoides looks like a weaver ant, with a pinched body and 2 black spots mimicking eyes on the side of its head, and it steals ant brood to pick up the colony's scent, though it generally steers clear of the nests. In Australia, three blue butterflies, the common, bright and purple oak-blues, depend on the ants and occur only where they are established.
didYouKnow: The smell-processing centres in a weaver ant's brain are arranged in clusters, a feature also seen in honeybees.

quiz.prompt: What do weaver ants use to stitch leaves together?
choices: Sticky sap collected from the trees they live in
quiz.explanation: Workers hold larvae against the leaf seams, and the larvae release silk threads.

quiz.prompt: What colour is a weaver ant queen?
choices: Bright red with yellow stripes along the abdomen
quiz.explanation: Queens are usually greenish-brown, giving the species its name smaragdina, meaning emerald.

quiz.prompt: Where does the oldest written record of using weaver ants against pests come from?
choices: Sri Lanka, where they guarded coffee plantations
quiz.explanation: It comes from China in 304 CE, where the ants protected citrus trees.

name: Common Wombat
range: Southeastern Australia, Tasmania and the Bass Strait islands
tagline: A burrowing marsupial with cube-shaped droppings
lede: The common wombat is a barrel-shaped Australian marsupial and a tireless digger that spends its days underground and its nights grazing. It is also famous for something unusual: its droppings come out as cubes.
home:
Common wombats live in the cooler, better-watered parts of southern and eastern Australia, including Victoria and Tasmania, and in mountain districts as far north as southern Queensland. In the south they can be found at any elevation, but in the north only in higher, mountainous country. They use a wide range of habitats, from rainforest, eucalyptus forest and woodland to alpine grassland, heathland and coast, and in some areas they graze in open fields alongside cattle and sheep.

Around 1.3 million are thought to remain in the wild, but more than two thirds of them live on islands, mostly Tasmania. On the mainland the species once ranged from South Australia's Limestone Coast across Victoria and along the Great Dividing Range, but its range and numbers have shrunk by more than half since European settlement, leaving populations in isolated pockets.
anatomy:
Wombats are sturdy and low-slung, with small ears and eyes, a large bald nose and short, strong legs ending in long claws. Their thick, coarse fur varies from light brown to grey and black. Size differs between the 3 subspecies. Mainland wombats average about 1 metre long and 27 kg, with the biggest reaching 1.2 metres and 35 kg. Tasmanian wombats average 85 cm and 20 kg, and Flinders Island wombats are the smallest, at around 75 cm.

Unlike any other marsupial, the wombat has a single pair of upper and lower incisors, and its teeth never stop growing. The structure of the enamel keeps a self-sharpening ridge on them, ideal for grazing tough native grasses.
life:
Common wombats are solitary and territorial, each living and feeding in an established home range. There they dig a tunnel system, with tunnels 2 to 20 metres long, many side branches and often more than one entrance, and build nests of sticks, leaves and grass. A wombat usually has several burrows and switches the one it sleeps in every 1 to 9 days, though more than one wombat may nest in the same burrow. Many stay with the same burrows for life, unless farmers or other animals force them out or the burrow is destroyed.

They are herbivores, eating mainly grass, snow tussocks and other plants. They usually feed at night, but in cool weather they also come out in the early morning or late afternoon. Captive wombats are fed a range of vegetables too.
family:
The common wombat breeds mainly in winter and can breed every 2 years, producing a single joey. After a short pregnancy of about 20 to 30 days, the newborn spends around 5 months in its mother's pouch. When it finally leaves, it weighs between 3.5 and 6.5 kg.

The joey is weaned at 12 to 15 months and is usually independent by 18 months. Wombats live about 15 years on average in the wild and 20 in captivity. Their main predators are quolls, Tasmanian devils, dingoes and eagles.
remarkable: Wombats have been called ecological engineers. Their digging turns over and aerates the soil, helping plants grow, and their burrows become shelter for a remarkable range of other animals, including reptiles, rodents, rabbits, echidnas, wallabies, birds and even koalas. Wombats are usually fairly tolerant of these non-threatening lodgers.
outlook:
The common wombat is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, but it still faces serious pressures, largely from people. Sarcoptic mange is widespread and remains the most troublesome problem, and wildlife carers regularly treat wombats in the field. Habitat loss and roadkill also take a toll, and wombats carry ticks and other parasites.

In Victoria, a $1 bounty from 1926 to 1966 branded wombats as farm pests for their burrowing and foraging, and wiped them out across much of their former range. The species had no protection in Victoria until 2020, and culling under licence there and in the Australian Capital Territory kills as many as 2,482 a year. In Tasmania, overall wombat counts rose between 1985 and 2019.
people:
The common wombat is also known as the bare-nosed wombat, after its large hairless nose. It was first described scientifically by George Shaw in 1800.

Today it is protected by law in South Australia under the National Parks and Wildlife Act 1972, in Queensland under the Nature Conservation Act 1992 and in New South Wales under the Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016. The treatment of mange by volunteer carers has become a big part of how people help wild wombats.
relatives:
The common wombat is one of 3 living wombat species and the only surviving member of its genus, Vombatus. Its 3 subspecies were confirmed in 2019: the hirsute wombat of the mainland; the Tasmanian wombat, estimated at 840,000 animals in 2023; and the Bass Strait wombat, once found across the Bass Strait islands but now restricted to Flinders Island and to Maria Island, where it was introduced, with an estimated 74,000 in 2023.

An extinct relative, Hackett's wombat, lived in southwestern Australia. It was about the same size, averaging 30 kg, and died out at the end of the Late Pleistocene.
didYouKnow: Wombats appear to mate lying on their sides.

quiz.prompt: What shape are common wombat droppings?
choices: Flat discs, which they stack on rocks to mark territory
quiz.explanation: Wombat dung is famously cube-shaped.

quiz.prompt: How long does a wombat joey stay in the pouch?
choices: About 3 years, until it is fully grown
quiz.explanation: Joeys spend around five months in the pouch before leaving it.

quiz.prompt: What is the most troublesome problem facing bare-nosed wombats?
choices: Competition with rabbits for burrows across the mainland
quiz.explanation: Sarcoptic mange is widespread and is the most problematic issue for the species.

name: Red King Crab
range: North Pacific from the Sea of Japan to Alaska; introduced to the Barents Sea
tagline: A giant crab that crossed a continent by plane
lede: With legs spanning up to 1.8 metres, the red king crab is the largest of the king crabs and the most prized by fishers. Oddly, it is named for the colour it turns when cooked: alive, it is more of a burgundy.
home:
The red king crab is native to the cold waters of the North Pacific and nearby seas, from the Bering Sea south to the Gulf of Alaska, and off the Kamchatka Peninsula, in the Sea of Okhotsk and in the Sea of Japan. It has been seen in water from −1.8 to 12.8 °C, though 3.2 to 5.5 °C is typical, and young crabs prefer it below 6 °C.

Where it lives depends on its age. Newly hatched larvae stay in shallow water, where food and protection are plentiful. After about 2 years, young crabs move to depths of 20 to 50 metres and gather in tight groups of hundreds, a habit called podding. Adults usually live more than 200 metres down on sand and mud.
anatomy:
Its shell can reach 28 cm across, and it can weigh up to 12.7 kg. Males grow larger than females. Today, few crabs exceed 17 cm across the shell, and the average male landed in the Bering Sea weighs 2.9 kg.

The crab breathes with 5 sets of gills, tucked into two chambers under the shell. A paddle-like appendage beats back and forth to pull water in from behind the walking legs and push it out beside the mouth, and fine hairs filter out debris. It can clear sediment and parasites from its rear gills by moving its small fifth pair of legs. Its blood carries oxygen with haemocyanin, a copper-based pigment that turns from colourless to blue when it picks up oxygen.
life:
Red king crabs spend most of their lives in deep water, where they feed. In the Barents Sea, studies of its diet show it acting as a high-level predator on the seabed, and some evidence suggests it eats the egg masses of capelin, an important food for cod.

In its native range it has many enemies, including Pacific cod, walleye pollock, halibut, several kinds of flatfish, sculpins, Greenland turbot, Pacific salmon and herring, sharks and rays, sea otters and seals. Its growth depends on temperature: it moults slowly below 8 °C, and quite quickly at around 12 °C. It copes well with changes in salinity, but slightly more acidic water, at pH 7.8 rather than 8.0, slows its growth and eventually kills it.
family:
Mature females must stay in warmer water, near 4 °C, so their eggs develop in time to hatch, while males stay in colder water, near 1.5 °C, to save energy. In winter or early spring the crabs migrate towards shallower water to mate, and in May females move into shallow coastal areas to moult and spawn, with males joining them before moulting.

From mid-June to mid-November, the crabs return to fairly deep water below the summer thermocline. When it breaks down, they move back to intermediate depths, where they stay until the females release the eggs fertilised in the previous spawning. Juveniles tolerate low salinity slightly better than adults.
remarkable: In the 1960s, the Soviet Union decided to give Europe a valuable new catch by moving red king crabs from the North Pacific to the Murmansk Fjord on the Barents Sea. Crabs sent overland died on the way, so a batch was flown in instead, and it survived, bred and spread. First found in Norway in 1977, the crab had reached North Cape by the mid-1990s and has since reached Svalbard, and some scientists think it is advancing about 50 km a year. One was even caught south of Bergen in 2009. An important natural predator, the giant Pacific octopus, does not live in European waters.
outlook:
In its native Far East coastal waters, the red king crab has been declining steadily for unclear reasons. Overfishing, warmer water and more predation by fish have all been suggested, and US fishing controls set in the 1980s and 2000s have failed to stop the fall.

In the Barents Sea, by contrast, its population is increasing tremendously. Environmentalists and fishers there worry that it eats everything it comes across, 'creating a desert' on the seabed, and they fear what will happen if it reaches the cod breeding grounds off Lofoten. Fishers also complain that its claws ruin nets and long lines.
people:
The red king crab is the most coveted king crab on the market and the most expensive by weight. It is caught mostly in the Bering Sea and Norton Sound in Alaska, and although it is hard to catch, it is one of the most popular crabs to eat. It is also called the Kamchatka crab or Alaskan king crab, and in Norway, because the Soviets introduced it, it is sometimes known as 'Stalin's crab'.

East of North Cape, Norway and Russia manage the crab jointly through a fisheries commission that sets quotas, and in 2006 only 259 Norwegian fishermen were allowed to catch it there. Processing waste can make up 69% of the catch, and enzymes from the crab's digestive gland interest various industries. A red king crab even appears as a boss in the video game Another Crab's Treasure.
relatives:
Paralithodes camtschaticus is the largest of the king crabs, and its species name refers to Kamchatka, one of its native strongholds. It is the most valuable of several king crab species sold commercially.

In January 2022, fishers in the United Kingdom reported catching red king crabs, raising fears of a new invasion, but the animals turned out to be a native species, Lithodes maja.
didYouKnow: A red king crab's heartbeat is set by a cluster of just 9 nerve cells attached to the wall of its heart.

quiz.prompt: Why is the red king crab called 'red'?
choices: It lives in the Red Sea
Its eggs glow red in the deep, dark water where it lives
quiz.explanation: Living crabs are more burgundy; the name comes from their cooked colour.

quiz.prompt: How were red king crabs brought to the Barents Sea?
choices: Flown in by the Soviet Union
They walked along the seabed around Siberia by themselves
quiz.explanation: Crabs sent overland died, so the Soviets flew in a batch that survived and spread.

quiz.prompt: What colour does the crab's haemocyanin turn when it carries oxygen?
choices: Bright yellow, like the copper inside it
quiz.explanation: Haemocyanin changes from colourless to blue when oxygenated.
